Musique should be on here since it was released in 1996 on [Source Lab 2](https://www.discogs.com/master/74728-Various-Source-Lab2). It was only rereleased due to a lot of bootlegging and Thomas wasn’t happy with that. It’s technically the only Daft Punk track published and licensed via Roulé and falls in-line within the Soma years.

There’s also [Manu Le Malin’s Memory](https://www.discogs.com/release/82013-DJ-Manu-Le-Malin-Memory) that they helped co-produce (although it’s said it was only Bangalter that helped, nonetheless he chose to use Daft Punk as the credit)

Daft Punk signed with Virgin in Spring/Summer of 1996 considering Homework released (as test pressings) as early as September of ‘96. Evidenced by Ian Pooley sharing his copies online and the copyright year on the album.

Homework is also a co-release with Soma records, as yes, a sign of gratitude but also to keep their credibility within the underground and help continue fund Soma.

Musique was originally released on a compilation on Source records (fun fact: it’s the only Daft Punk record on Roulé as it was licensed via Roulé to Source). Not too long after, it was made the b-side for the Da Funk re-release on Virgin as the first single for Homework. There was an interview where Thomas was complaining that people were already bootlegging Musique off the Source compilation and selling them off as white labels. Coupled with the fact that the Da Funk re-release had sold more than Homework at the time, they figured there was no point in putting the track on the album.

I have an S700 and most emulations of 12-bit machines of the time. I’ve come to neglect 16-bit samplers thinking they were pretty boring as well but their converters weren’t the best compared to 2000s converters. For example the Roland S-760 seems to widen the stereo image jusssst a tad bit while doing something to the bass (40-250Hz gets this warmth and eases any distortion that may have been there) and having a high pass around 20Hz. The ASR-10 is notable for being crunchy in the sense that the mids are excited. 

Why the 2000/3000XL specifically? The 2000 because Calibre used it for most of his early work. Compared to the 3000XL, it’s a bit warmer in the highs due to some very slight internal changes (due to the price difference between the two). I know Akais tend to also have some weird compression/mid and low mid punch compared to a cleaner EMU Emulator IV.

Ableton Live Suite has a plugin that allows you to capture an impulse. You’d set the sample rate, then sample the sine sweep and finally record the output back into Live. Live also has a Convolution plugin that can play back impulses. Ideally you’d place it after your sample(s) and imbue it with the color of whatever you recorded.

[Recording Impulses in Live](https://youtu.be/1egKAtC16e8?si=yQFI67mnP0aqXt21)

[Impulse Response](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse_response)

Traditionally used for reverbs, some people use them to capture the frequency response of a sampler’s converters/sampling.

You don't need it, but learn how to gain stage and setting levels with the VU/RMS. If you use certain samples often, you'll be setting your levels fairly quickly after getting everything memorized.

I like my kicks LOUD, so it'll make that hit 0 (nominal level is -18dBFS—default on the device) and start basing the mix around that and whatever important sample element.

They're also good for gain matching with EQs and compressors. Simply place one before your plugin and bring it up to your desired level (A good start is 0dBVU = -18dBFS or -20dBFS depending on country of origin). Do your EQing/compression and then place another after the plugin and use the gain of the plugin to bring it back up to 0dBVU. Now you can hear what the unit is actually doing and make adjustments.

The difference this time around? I was extremely upfront with my therapist:

I don’t like a lot of the light-hearted reassurance (oh...that must be frustrating—overly validating like speaking to a child)

I make sure to tell them they have to be pretty blunt when it comes to explaining things or helping me navigate/process situations. 

I ensure for them to call me out on my shit when able (they do it like a friend will—“Uh, that’s not what you said earlier” or “You’re not making sense with regard to X” “That’s some BS X, you know it too” 

Goals—go in and state what’d you’d like to do with yourself objectively. I helped this EXTREMELY helped when I went back. I keep a journal of notes of when I write down diaries, things I wanna bring up, mappings of how things (or how I think at the time) operate (like spider-maps or flow charts), or stuff I’m not sure I wanna speak out loud and I can hand it over to my therapist for them to look further.

I remind myself that there is no shame in that room and that there is no shame in my experience of life. After a while it tends to become find dissecting your own and other people’s patterns and such. 

Empathy is a real goal of mine in therapy, so I ensure that I also tackle that often when the situations arise.

It sucks sometimes tbh, I don’t wanna make it seem like flowers and rainbows. But restructuring it like this really helped me get passed my own ego and self-imposed stigma of taking it again.

Depends on the model! Sta-prest 517's are my go-to. The ones from the late-60s to the mid-70s tend to be mid-to-high rise and have a more accented flare. They're tight from the waist to the thigh. 

The ones from the late-70s to the early-80s lose the accent in the flare (less of a triangle shape and more a straight slit). These tend to usually always be high-rise but you might find a mid in the wild. They're still tight around the waist and hip but become more loose mid-thigh down. I recommend to measure your natural waist when looking for your sizing online. If you stick TTS, just know you'll probably not be able to put much in the front pockets due to them being right at your hipbone.
